editorials.titleTr: Opinion: Retail investors shed tears as insiders pocket billions on FDA approval—is this really serving the public interest?
summaryTr: Stock price fluctuates due to lobbying for drug agency approval, causing losses for small investors
Concerns over reduced allegations as prosecution changes indictment policy
Political interference spreads controversy over damage to public interest
editorials.bodyTr:
The case involving allegations that Justice Minister nominee Kim Seung-won intervened in requests for new drug approvals, resulting in stock price fluctuations that caused losses to numerous small investors, presents serious concerns about fairness and accountability. The prosecution's sudden reversal of its indictment policy and the political establishment's response to this matter warrant critical scrutiny.

What troubles observers most is not merely the allegations themselves, but the broader implications for trust in institutions. When high-ranking government officials are suspected of leveraging their positions for corporate gain, and ordinary citizens bear the financial consequences, the integrity of our regulatory systems comes into question. The involvement of a justice minister nominee in such matters strikes at the heart of judicial independence and the rule of law.

The prosecution's change in direction raises difficult questions about investigative consistency and political influence. Whether motivated by pressure from political circles or other considerations, such reversals undermine public confidence in the impartiality of law enforcement. Citizens deserve to know that investigations into powerful figures proceed according to consistent principles, not shifting calculations.

Political leaders bear responsibility for addressing these concerns transparently. Dismissing accusations as witch hunts or downplaying the harm to small investors only deepens public skepticism. The political community must demonstrate that it takes such matters seriously and that no one, regardless of rank or connections, stands above accountability.

This situation serves as a reminder that a functioning democracy depends on institutional integrity at every level. Only through honest examination of these allegations and consistent application of investigative standards can public trust be restored.

editorial.body: 입력 업데이트 종합 26면 북한군의 군사분계선(MDL) 월선이 반복되고 있다. 북한이 MDL 일대에 도로와 진지를 구축하면서 상습 월선 구간까지 생겼다. 우리 군은 열상감시장비(TOD) 등을 MDL에 가깝게 전진 배치하는 방안을 검토 중이다. 월선 여부를 정확히 식별해 불필요한 경고사격과 오판을 줄이겠다는 취지다. 필요한 조치지만, 묻지 않을 수 없다. 북한군이 자꾸 선을 넘는데 우리는 안 막는 것인가, 못 막는 것인가. 전선지역에서 대규모 병력 투입돼 작업 중인 북한군.[합동참모본부] 문제는 월선이 실수가 아니라는 점이다. 북한은 전방 요새화 작업을 하며 도로와 진지를 만들고 지뢰까지 매설해 병력을 정기적으로 이동시키고 있다. 일부 이동로가 MDL 남쪽을 지나 상습 월선과 경고사격이 반복되는 구조다. 우리 군의 대응도 달라져야 한다. 하지만 그간 군이 보여준 행보는 우려스러웠다. 지난해 말 국방부 관계자가 북한군의 MDL 침범 시 경고사격에 앞서 상황평가를 면밀히 하라고 지시했고, 군 수뇌부도 기계적 대응 대신 상황에 따른 판단을 주문한 사실이 드러났다. 최전방 ‘빈총 경계’ 실태까지 알려지면서 전방 부대가 경고사격을 자제해 온 정황도 알려졌다. 군이 소극적으로 임할수록 상대가 우리 경계 태세를 시험할 가능성은 커진다. 우리 군이 북한과의 충돌 기피에만 몰두했던 것은 아닌지 돌아봐야 한다. 북한은 최근 노동당 규약에서 ‘평화통일’과 ‘민족대단결’ 등 통일 관련 표현을 삭제하며 ‘적대적 두 국가’ 노선을 한층 공식화했다. 대남 통일 노선 폐기와 최전방 요새화가 같은 방향을 가리키고 있다. 가뜩이나 북한은 핵미사일 개발을 강화하는 상황이다. 이런 북한을 상대로 우리 군이 최전방의 경계를 느슨하게 하는 것은 우리 스스로 안보의 둑을 허무는 일이 된다. 감시장비 전진 배치만으로는 부족하다. 북한의 MDL 침범을 용인하지 않겠다는 원칙을 분명히 하고, 유엔군사령부와 감시·대응 체계도 긴밀히 조율해야 한다. 강신철 국방부 장관 후보자는 취임 후 MDL 문제를 최우선 현안으로 삼아 흐트러진 군의 기강과 느슨해진 대북 경계 태세를 바로잡아야 할 것이다. 안보는 말이나 양보가 아니라 단호한 원칙과 압도적 대응력으로 지키는 것이다.

우리 군은 감시장비 전진배치로 오판을 줄이려 하지만 근본 대책 부족하다.

editorial.titleTr: North Korea's Repeated MDL Violations: Can They Be Stopped?
summaryTr: North Korean troops are repeatedly crossing the Military Demarcation Line while constructing roads and fortifications.
Our military is attempting to reduce misunderstandings through forward deployment of surveillance equipment, but fundamental countermeasures are lacking.
We must not lower our guard against North Korea's clearly hostile stance, or security threats will escalate.
editorial.bodyTr:
North Korean soldiers repeatedly cross the Military Demarcation Line. As North Korea constructs roads and fortifications around the MDL, certain crossing points have become habitual. Our military is reviewing plans to deploy thermal observation devices and other surveillance equipment closer to the MDL. The stated goal is to accurately identify crossings and reduce unnecessary warning shots and misjudgments. While a necessary measure, one must ask: Is our military unwilling or unable to stop North Korean forces from repeatedly crossing the line?

The fundamental problem is that these crossings are not accidental. North Korea is systematically fortifying its forward positions, constructing roads and trenches, laying mines, and regularly moving troops. Some of these movement routes pass south of the MDL, creating a cycle of habitual crossings and warning shots. Our military response must evolve accordingly.

Yet the military's approach thus far is troubling. Last year, Defense Ministry officials instructed troops to conduct careful situational assessments before warning shots when North Korean forces breach the MDL, and military leadership ordered judgment based on circumstances rather than mechanical responses. Reports have emerged that forward units have exercised restraint in firing warning shots, with some units experiencing so-called "empty gun patrols." The more passively our military acts, the more likely the adversary will test our readiness. We must examine whether our military has been preoccupied solely with avoiding confrontation with North Korea.

North Korea has recently removed references to "peaceful reunification" and "national solidarity" from its party charter, formally solidifying its "hostile two-state" policy. The abandonment of inter-Korean unification lines and forward fortification point in the same direction. This comes as North Korea intensifies nuclear and missile development. For our military to relax vigilance at the front lines against such an adversary would be to undermine our own security.

Deploying surveillance equipment forward is insufficient. We must establish a clear principle that we will not tolerate North Korean violations of the MDL and coordinate closely with United Nations Command on monitoring and response systems. Defense Minister nominee Kang Shin-chul must make the MDL issue his top priority upon taking office and restore discipline to our military and strengthen our eroded deterrence posture against North Korea. Security is not maintained through words or concessions but through firm principles and overwhelming response capability.

leanScore.label: Strongly conservative
leanScore.rationale: 북한의 MDL 침범을 '우리 스스로 안보의 둑을 허무는 일'으로 규정하며 군의 소극적 대응을 비판하고, 단호한 원칙과 압도적 대응력을 강조하는 강경한 안보-대북 프레이밍이 전면적으로 드러남.

editorial.title: Hollow reforms
editorial.body: Political caution weakens pension overhaul, leaving future generations with rising costs In South Korea, the basic pension has a curious tendency to become less ambitious as it approaches the ballot box. The closer a proposed overhaul gets to voters, the smaller it seems to become. The Lee Jae Myung administration began with an ambitious promise to make the basic pension “heavier at the bottom and lighter at the top” in terms of benefits. On Tuesday, however, the government delivered a much narrower change. It kept the politically convenient 70 percent coverage rule and made only limited adjustments to payouts. Korea faces a difficult pension dilemma: protecting a growing number of impoverished elderly people without allowing public finances to buckle under demographic pressure. The latest plan handles the first concern at the margins and largely postpones the second. Under the new scheme starting next April, monthly payouts for the bottom 30 percent will rise to 380,000 won ($279), while the 30 to 45 percent bracket will receive an inflation-adjusted 359,000 won. Payments for the upper 45 to 70 percent remain frozen at 350,000 won, and the spousal reduction for lower-income couples will ease from 20 to 10 percent. That is a modest redistribution within an expanding system. Freezing payments for the upper tier saves about 170 billion won, while differentiated payouts require an additional 465 billion won. The annual basic pension budget will consequently rise by about 11 percent, from 23.1 trillion won this year to 25.7 trillion won next year. The compromise is especially conspicuous because the Ministry of Health and Welfare had considered replacing the 70 percent rule with a median-income threshold, eventually reducing eligibility to 80 percent by 2030. After a scheduled briefing by Health and Welfare Minister Jeong Eun-kyeong was abruptly canceled on Aug. 27, however, the final proposal dropped eligibility reform altogether. The political logic is hardly mysterious. With public sentiment already unsettled by real estate tax changes and the president’s approval ratings weakening, reducing pension eligibility would have imposed another immediate political cost. The 70 percent rule has become harder to justify as a proxy for need. Some older single workers earning around 4.68 million won a month can qualify if they have no other assets, while married couples with combined annual income approaching 100 million won may also fall within the threshold. Meanwhile, Korea still has one of the highest elderly poverty rates in the OECD. Adding 30,000 won a month to the poorest group will hardly transform that picture, particularly when basic pension payments can interact awkwardly with minimum livelihood benefits. Then comes the demographic ledger. Basic pension recipients have grown from about 2 million in 2015 to 7.79 million this year. Their number is projected to reach 13.3 million by 2050, while spending could rise to 46 trillion won, according to the Korea Development Institute. That trajectory demands a clearer definition of whom the basic pension is meant to support. Eligibility should gradually move toward an objective median-income benchmark rather than a fixed share of the elderly population. Savings from narrower coverage should be redirected toward seniors facing genuine hardship. The system should also evolve alongside the maturing national pension fund and voluntary private retirement savings. The Lee administration has postponed the difficult part of reform. That may ease political friction for the moment, but demographic arithmetic does not disappear because it chooses to defer it. Sustainability cannot be achieved by passing a diluted bill. Preserving broad entitlements while gutting core reforms is a compromise in name only, leaving future generations to settle the bill. summaryTr: 한국의 연금개혁안이 유권자 투표를 앞두고 축소되고 있으며, 70% 보장률 규칙은 그대로 유지된다.
이번 소폭의 개편안은 하위 30%의 수령액을 월 3만 원 인상하는 한편 상위 계층 혜택은 동결했다.
정부는 기초연금 비용이 2050년까지 46조 원으로 3배 증가할 수 있다는 전망에도 구조적 개혁을 미루고 있다.
editorial.bodyTr:
한국에서 기초연금은 투표함에 가까워질수록 덜 야심 차지는 이상한 경향을 보인다. 제안된 개혁이 유권자에게 가까워질수록 그 규모는 작아지는 것 같다. 이재명 행정부는 기초연금을 혜택 측면에서 "아래는 무겁게, 위는 가볍게" 만들겠다는 야심 찬 공약으로 시작했다. 그러나 화요일 정부는 훨씬 제한적인 변화를 내놓았다. 정치적으로 편리한 70% 보장 규칙을 유지했고 급여 조정만 제한적으로 이루어졌다.

한국은 어려운 연금 딜레마에 직면해 있다. 증가하는 저소득 노인층을 보호하면서도 인구 구조적 압박으로 공공재정이 무너지지 않도록 하는 것이다. 최신 계획은 첫 번째 우려에는 한계적으로만 대처하고 두 번째 우려는 대체로 미루고 있다.

내년 4월부터 시행되는 새로운 제도 아래에서 하위 30%의 월 급여는 38만 원으로 인상되고, 30~45% 구간은 물가 조정된 35만 9천 원을 받게 된다. 상위 45~70%의 급여는 35만 원에서 동결되며, 저소득 부부의 배우자 감액은 20%에서 10%로 완화된다. 이는 확대되는 시스템 내에서의 소박한 재분배이다. 상위층 급여 동결로 약 1,700억 원이 절감되는 반면, 차등 급여로는 추가로 4,650억 원이 필요하다. 따라서 기초연금의 연간 예산은 올해 23조 1천억 원에서 내년 25조 7천억 원으로 약 11% 증가할 것이다.

이러한 타협이 특히 두드러지는 이유는 보건복지부가 70% 규칙을 중위소득 기준으로 대체하여 2030년까지 보장률을 80%로 단계적으로 축소하는 방안을 검토했기 때문이다. 그러나 8월 27일 정경은 보건복지부 장관의 예정된 브리핑이 갑자기 취소된 후, 최종 제안에서는 보장률 개편이 완전히 빠졌다. 정치적 논리는 거의 신비로울 것이 없다. 공공 여론이 이미 부동산세 변화로 불안정하고 대통령 지지율이 약해진 상황에서 연금 보장률 축소는 또 다른 즉각적인 정치적 비용을 초래했을 것이기 때문이다.

70% 규칙은 필요성을 나타내는 대리로 정당화하기가 점점 더 어려워졌다. 월 약 468만 원을 버는 일부 고령 독신 근로자는 다른 자산이 없다면 적격이 될 수 있고, 연 소득이 약 1억 원에 가까운 기혼 부부도 기준선 내에 들어갈 수 있다. 한편 한국은 여전히 OECD에서 가장 높은 노인 빈곤율을 기록하고 있다. 가장 가난한 계층에 월 3만 원을 추가하는 것은 특히 기초연금 급여가 최저생계비 급여와 어색하게 상호작용할 수 있을 때 그 그림을 크게 바꾸지 못할 것이다.

그 다음은 인구 통계 장부이다. 기초연금 수급자는 2015년 약 200만 명에서 올해 779만 명으로 증가했다. 이들의 수는 2050년까지 1,330만 명에 도달할 것으로 예상되며, 한국개발연구원에 따르면 지출은 46조 원까지 증가할 수 있다. 그러한 궤적은 기초연금이 어떤 계층을 지원하는 것인지에 대한 보다 명확한 정의를 요구한다. 보장률은 점진적으로 노인 인구의 고정 비율이 아닌 객관적 중위소득 기준을 향해 움직여야 한다. 좁혀진 보장범위에서 나온 절감액은 진정한 어려움에 직면한 고령자들을 향해 재배분되어야 한다. 이 시스템은 또한 성숙해지는 국민연금 기금과 자발적 개인 퇴직 저축과 함께 발전해야 한다.

이재명 행정부는 개혁의 어려운 부분을 미뤄왔다. 그것이 당분간 정치적 마찰을 완화할 수 있지만, 인구 통계 산술은 그것이 연기되었다고 해서 사라지지 않는다. 희석된 법안을 통해 지속 가능성을 달성할 수 없다. 광범한 혜택을 유지하면서 핵심 개혁을 손상시키는 것은 명목상의 타협일 뿐이며, 미래 세대에게 빚을 정산하도록 남겨둔다.

editorials.title: Hollow reforms
editorials.body: Political caution weakens pension overhaul, leaving future generations with rising costs In South Korea, the basic pension has a curious tendency to become less ambitious as it approaches the ballot box. The closer a proposed overhaul gets to voters, the smaller it seems to become. The Lee Jae Myung administration began with an ambitious promise to make the basic pension “heavier at the bottom and lighter at the top” in terms of benefits. On Tuesday, however, the government delivered a much narrower change. It kept the politically convenient 70 percent coverage rule and made only limited adjustments to payouts. Korea faces a difficult pension dilemma: protecting a growing number of impoverished elderly people without allowing public finances to buckle under demographic pressure. The latest plan handles the first concern at the margins and largely postpones the second. Under the new scheme starting next April, monthly payouts for the bottom 30 percent will rise to 380,000 won ($279), while the 30 to 45 percent bracket will receive an inflation-adjusted 359,000 won. Payments for the upper 45 to 70 percent remain frozen at 350,000 won, and the spousal reduction for lower-income couples will ease from 20 to 10 percent. That is a modest redistribution within an expanding system. Freezing payments for the upper tier saves about 170 billion won, while differentiated payouts require an additional 465 billion won. The annual basic pension budget will consequently rise by about 11 percent, from 23.1 trillion won this year to 25.7 trillion won next year. The compromise is especially conspicuous because the Ministry of Health and Welfare had considered replacing the 70 percent rule with a median-income threshold, eventually reducing eligibility to 80 percent by 2030. After a scheduled briefing by Health and Welfare Minister Jeong Eun-kyeong was abruptly canceled on Aug. 27, however, the final proposal dropped eligibility reform altogether. The political logic is hardly mysterious. With public sentiment already unsettled by real estate tax changes and the president’s approval ratings weakening, reducing pension eligibility would have imposed another immediate political cost. The 70 percent rule has become harder to justify as a proxy for need. Some older single workers earning around 4.68 million won a month can qualify if they have no other assets, while married couples with combined annual income approaching 100 million won may also fall within the threshold. Meanwhile, Korea still has one of the highest elderly poverty rates in the OECD. Adding 30,000 won a month to the poorest group will hardly transform that picture, particularly when basic pension payments can interact awkwardly with minimum livelihood benefits. Then comes the demographic ledger. Basic pension recipients have grown from about 2 million in 2015 to 7.79 million this year. Their number is projected to reach 13.3 million by 2050, while spending could rise to 46 trillion won, according to the Korea Development Institute. That trajectory demands a clearer definition of whom the basic pension is meant to support. Eligibility should gradually move toward an objective median-income benchmark rather than a fixed share of the elderly population. Savings from narrower coverage should be redirected toward seniors facing genuine hardship. The system should also evolve alongside the maturing national pension fund and voluntary private retirement savings. The Lee administration has postponed the difficult part of reform. That may ease political friction for the moment, but demographic arithmetic does not disappear because it chooses to defer it. Sustainability cannot be achieved by passing a diluted bill. Preserving broad entitlements while gutting core reforms is a compromise in name only, leaving future generations to settle the bill.
